Key ideas

Modelling resistance in series circuits

Definitions

Resistance: a measure of how much an object or material impedes the flow of current measured in units of ohms (Ω)
Ohmic resistor: a material that gives a straight line I–V graph; i.e. it obeys Ohm’s law
Ohm’s law: for a particular type of material that gives a straight-line characteristic I vs V graph, meaning that V = IR always holds for that material
Equivalent resistance: the value of a single resistor that could replace a number of individual resistors to give the same effect in the circuit
Series circuit: when circuit components are connected one after the other in a continuous loop, so that the same current passes through each component

Formulas

Formula 5C–1 Ohm’s law
V=IRorR=VIV = IR \quad\text{or}\quad R = \frac{V}{I}V=IRorR=IV​

RequivalentR_{\text{equivalent}}Requivalent​Equivalent resistance for resistors in series (Ω\mathrm{\Omega}Ω)R1,R2,…,RnR_1, R_2, \dots, R_nR1​,R2​,…,Rn​Resistance of each resistor (Ω\mathrm{\Omega}Ω)

New knowledgeWhat is electrical resistance?

Modelling resistance in series circuits

You have seen that the energy dissipated in a circuit can be understood using concepts of charge, current and potential difference.

These quantities are related: as the energy supplied to a circuit increases, the amount of charge that flows increases.

Sometimes the relationship between these quantities is simple, and other times it is more complex.

Let’s start with a simple circuit.

Figure 5C–3 Left: A simple circuit showing a light bulb connected to a variable voltage power supply Right: By connecting an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel as shown, the I–V (current vs potential difference) data for the bulb can be easily obtained and graphed.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 445
5C

New knowledgeWhat is electrical resistance?

Modelling resistance in series circuits

In Figure 5C–3 (left), a light bulb is connected to a power supply.

The potential difference supplied can be varied from 0 to 12 V.

When the switch is closed, current flows through the bulb.

As the potential difference is increased, the current will increase too.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 446
5C

New knowledgeWhat is electrical resistance?

Modelling resistance in series circuits

The light will get brighter as more energy is supplied (recall from Section 5B that E = VIt).

But are the two quantities, current and potential difference, related to each other in a simple mathematical way?

To find out, a voltmeter and an ammeter must be added to the circuit as shown in Figure 5C–3 (right).

The potential difference can now be increased in steps from 0 to 12 V and the value of current recorded for each step.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 447
5C

New knowledgeWhat is electrical resistance?

Modelling resistance in series circuits

Plotting a graph of current against potential difference (Figure 5C–4) shows that as the potential difference is increased, the current increases too, but not in a uniform (or steady) way.

You can tell this because the graph is not a straight line; the gradient changes.

This is because the filament of the bulb gets hotter as more current passes through it, and hotter metals become more resistant to current flow.

Think of vibrations of thermal energy of the metal lattice ions getting in the way of the drifting electrons, like a rugby player with the ball trying to dodge while running through the opposition defence.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 448
5C

New knowledgeWhat is electrical resistance?

Modelling resistance in series circuits

If the defenders move more, it’s harder to dodge through without colliding.

If a similar circuit is set up where the heating effect is as small as possible, the I–V graph will be straight.

Figure 5C–5 (left) shows an example using a laboratory resistor.

The current now increases steadily as the potential difference rises, shown by the graph of I vs V (Figure 5C–5 right).

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 449

New knowledgeWhat is electrical resistance?

Modelling resistance in series circuits

The ratio of V to I for a component is called its resistance, R.

The unit of resistance is the ohm (given the Greek letter ‘omega’, Ω).

It is constant for some components such as an ohmic resistor and varies with current and temperature for others, such as a light bulb.

The relationship between potential difference and current is expressed by the equation below.

This is called Ohm’s law and it is more commonly expressed as: The laboratory resistor in Figure 5C–5 has a constant value for V I , so it has a constant gradient of the I–V graph or run 1 resistance of 3 Ω.

Note that this can be calculated from rise.

The value of V I for the light bulb changed as the current increased, showing that in this case, the resistance was not constant.

When a current of 0.5 A is flowing, the value of V I is 3 Ω, while at 1.0 A it is 5.0 Ω.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 4411
5C

New knowledgeSeries circuits: current, potential difference and resistance

Modelling resistance in series circuits

So far Ohm’s law, V = IR, has been used to analyse simple circuits with only one load component.

Many circuits contain several components, and their total or equivalent resistance must be found before the circuit can be analysed fully.

Components may be connected in series, in parallel or in a combination of the two.

Two or more components are said to be in series in a circuit if there is only one path for current to flow.

Figure 5C–6 In a series circuit, the same amount of current passes through each of the resistors and back to the battery — there is nowhere else for the electrons to go. The energy supplied by the battery (the potential difference) is shared between the resistors according to the resistance of each of them. The greater the resistance, the greater its share of the potential difference.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 4912
5C

New knowledgeSeries circuits: current, potential difference and resistance

Modelling resistance in series circuits

The components are connected in a chain, one after the other.

Note that for series circuits: • there is only one current path through R1, R2 and R3, so there must be the same current, I, in each. (Electrons do not stop anywhere on their way around the circuit.) • the sum of the potential differences across R1, R2, and R3 must equal the potential difference that the battery provides: Vsupply = V1 + V2 + V3 Using Ohm’s law repeatedly around this circuit gives R = V I for each resistor.

If you then add these up, you can find the equivalent resistance of the circuit.

V V V R equivalent = 1 1 2 1 3 O R 1 R 1 R 1 2 3 I I I 1 2 3 Therefore, for resistors in series, the total equivalent resistance of the combination is the sum of the individual resistances: If you connect batteries in series, the total potential difference is the sum of the individual potential differences.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 4913
5C

New knowledgePotential (or voltage) dividers: a useful series circuit

Modelling resistance in series circuits

A simple potential divider (or voltage divider) consists of two resistors in series.

The output potential difference is taken from the point between the two, as shown in Figure 5C–7.

By varying the values of each resistor, any number of volts can be supplied at the output from a fixed input.

Knowledge of series circuits and Ohm’s law are used to calculate the output as follows.

Figure 5C–7 Two resistors in series with a fixed voltage supply can be used to give any amount of output voltage, Vout, by varying the sizes of the resistors
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 5114
5C

New knowledgePotential (or voltage) dividers: a useful series circuit

Modelling resistance in series circuits

The total equivalent resistance, Requivalent, in this circuit is: Requivalent = R1 + R2 Using Ohm’s law (V = IR), the current, I, through R1 + R2 is given by: V V I = = in Equation 1 R R + R equivalent 1 2 Applying Ohm’s law to R2 gives: Vout = IR2 Equation 2 Substituting Equation 1 into Equation 2 gives: V V = in R out 2 1 R R 1 2 Which is usually written as: R 2 This ratio makes sense, as you know that in a series circuit the potential drop + R R 1 2 across each component depends on the resistance of that component.

So, the potential drop across R2 will be the same proportion of Vin as the proportion of R2 is in the whole circuit R1 + R2.

Resistors R1 and R2 ‘divide up’ the input volts Vin in proportion; hence the name for this arrangement: potential divider (sometimes called voltage divider).

By using variable resistors, or components that are sensitive to changes in temperature (thermistors) or light level (light-dependent resistors), Vout can be controlled to turn on or off refrigeration motors or streetlights at the appropriate temperature or level of darkness.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 5115

We doApplying Ohm’s law to a car headlight

Modelling resistance in series circuits
A car LED headlight is powered by a 12.0 V battery. Find the resistance of the car headlight when there is a current of 5.0 A through it, operating normally.
Key idea · Formula 5C–1 Ohm’s lawV=IRorR=VIV = IR \quad\text{or}\quad R = \frac{V}{I}V=IRorR=IV​

Working

Use Ohm’s law: V=IRV = IRV=IR
The potential difference is provided by the battery, so V=12.0V = 12.0V=12.0 V, and the current is given as I=5.0I = 5.0I=5.0 A.
The resistance, RRR, is given by:
R=VIR = \frac{V}{I}R=IV​
=12.05.0= \frac{12.0}{5.0}=5.012.0​
=2.4 Ω= 2.4\ \Omega=2.4 Ω
The resistance of the headlight is 2.4 Ω.
2.4 Ω

We doMeter readings in a circuit

Modelling resistance in series circuits
What would each of the meters read in this circuit? (circuit: 12 V battery, 4 kΩ resistor, two ammeters, voltmeter across resistor; see image)
Key idea · Formula 5C–1 Ohm’s lawV=IRorR=VIV = IR \quad\text{or}\quad R = \frac{V}{I}V=IRorR=IV​

Working

For a circuit with a single resistor, the entire potential difference from the battery is dissipated in the 4 kΩ resistor. So, the voltmeter will read 12 V.
The current can be calculated using Ohm’s law: V=IRV = IRV=IR
The potential difference is V=12V = 12V=12 V, and the resistance is R=4R = 4R=4 kΩ.
Rearrange the formula to find the current, III.
I=VRI = \frac{V}{R}I=RV​
=124×103= \frac{12}{4\times10^{3}}=4×10312​
=3×10−3= 3\times10^{-3}=3×10−3 A
It is a series circuit, so both ammeters will read 3 mA.
Voltmeter 12 V; both ammeters 3 mA

Modelling resistance in series circuits
Three resistors of 1 MΩ, 2 MΩ and 0.5 MΩ are connected in series and carry a current of 4.8 µA. Find the potential difference across the combination.
Key idea · Formula 5C–1 Ohm’s lawV=IRorR=VIV = IR \quad\text{or}\quad R = \frac{V}{I}V=IRorR=IV​

Working

First draw a circuit diagram, adding all the information from the question: (see image)
Apply the series resistance Formula 5C–2 to calculate the equivalent resistance of the series combination:
Requivalent=R1+R2+R3R_{\text{equivalent}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3Requivalent​=R1​+R2​+R3​
=1×106+2×106+0.5×106= 1\times10^{6} + 2\times10^{6} + 0.5\times10^{6}=1×106+2×106+0.5×106
=3.5×106 Ω= 3.5\times10^{6}\ \Omega=3.5×106 Ω
Apply Ohm’s law to find the potential difference:
Vtotal=IRequivalentV_{\text{total}} = IR_{\text{equivalent}}Vtotal​=IRequivalent​
=4.8×10−6×3.5×106= 4.8\times10^{-6} \times 3.5\times10^{6}=4.8×10−6×3.5×106
=16.8= 16.8=16.8 V
The potential difference across the series combination is 16.8 V.

We doUsing a potential divider

Modelling resistance in series circuits
A particular mobile phone requires a potential difference of up to 5 V to charge correctly. The only power supply available is a 12 V battery from a caravan. A physics student thinks of using a potential divider circuit to supply the required 5 V. If one available resistor is 1.0 kΩ, what should the second resistor in the potential divider be and how should they be arranged? The other resistors available are 0.8 kΩ, 1.2 kΩ and 1.4 kΩ. Show your reasoning and a labelled diagram. What other considerations should the student take into account before operating this set-up?
Key idea · Formula 5C–1 Ohm’s lawV=IRorR=VIV = IR \quad\text{or}\quad R = \frac{V}{I}V=IRorR=IV​

Working

First draw a diagram including all the information given in the question. (see image)
Consider whether the 1 kΩ resistor would be best placed as R1 or R2. Since 5 V required is less than half the 12 V available, put the 1 kΩ as R2 so the larger resistors can be in the top of the potential divider.
Using Formula 5C–3 we can calculate the required equivalent resistance:
R2Requivalent=VoutVin\frac{R_2}{R_{\text{equivalent}}} = \frac{V_{\text{out}}}{V_{\text{in}}}Requivalent​R2​​=Vin​Vout​​
1×103Rtotal=512\frac{1\times10^{3}}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{5}{12}Rtotal​1×103​=125​
Rtotal=125×103=2.4×103 ΩR_{\text{total}} = \frac{12}{5}\times10^{3} = 2.4\times10^{3}\ \OmegaRtotal​=512​×103=2.4×103 Ω
Now, because R1 and R2 are in series:
Rtotal=R1+R2R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2Rtotal​=R1​+R2​
Substitute into the formula:
2.4×103=R1+1×1032.4\times10^{3} = R_1 + 1\times10^{3}2.4×103=R1​+1×103
So: R1=1.4×103=1.4R_1 = 1.4\times10^{3} = 1.4R1​=1.4×103=1.4 kΩ
Among the other considerations is the amount of current the phone will draw while recharging: can the battery supply this without overheating, and can the resistors and the connecting wires handle this current without damage? Conversely, would the battery supply more current in this set-up than the phone can handle? More detailed understanding of these and other factors is needed, and experimenting with expensive items is not recommended.
R1 = 1.4 kΩ (top), R2 = 1.0 kΩ (output across R2)
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 52, Worked example 5C-528

Can the output potential difference, VoutV_{\text{out}}Vout​, of a potential divider ever be larger than the input potential difference, VinV_{\text{in}}Vin​? Explain your answer.
Consider the formula for potential dividers. The equivalent resistance of a series circuit, RequivalentR_{\text{equivalent}}Requivalent​, is always larger than the individual resistances; RnR_nRn​. Therefore, the ratio of resistances must be less than or equal to one. So, VoutVin=R2Requivalent≤1\frac{V_{\text{out}}}{V_{\text{in}}} = \frac{R_2}{R_{\text{equivalent}}} \leq 1Vin​Vout​​=Requivalent​R2​​≤1.
